claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The unmodified alloy exhibits radiation-induced precipitation under the stated fusion-relevant irradiation conditions.
The unmodified alloy exhibits measurable irradiation hardening under the stated conditions.
The proposed intervention is incorporation of approximately 1 vol% high-purity Y2O3 nanoparticles into the alloy.
Mechanical alloying and nanoparticle surface functionalization can produce a uniform Y2O3 dispersion while preventing agglomeration.
Controlled sintering or forging can retain the alloy's fine-grained structure after Y2O3 addition.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as stable irradiation-defect sinks.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles pin grain boundaries and stabilize the nanostructured grain-boundary network.
Y2O3 nanoparticles trap irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Trapping vacancies and interstitials reduces solute diffusion and agglomeration that would otherwise produce precipitates.
Nanoparticle-mediated microstructural stabilization prevents irradiation-induced hardening.
Grain-boundary stabilization by Y2O3 improves sinterability and practical bulk fabrication.
At approximately 8 dpa and 600–700°C, Y2O3 addition will reduce the radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction by at least 30% relative to the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa and 600–700°C, the modified alloy's hardness increase will remain below 10% of its baseline hardness.
The modified alloy will have better grain-boundary stability than the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will have improved sinterability and bulk fabricability relative to the unmodified alloy.
The claimed behavior is limited to energetic-particle irradiation up to approximately 8 dpa at 600–700°C.
